documentation.range: Tolypeutes matacus is found from eastern Bolivia and southwestern Brazil, south through the Gran Chaco of Paraguay, to Argentina, with San Luis province being its southernmost limit (Feijó et al. 2015, Ferreiro et al. 2022). The species was once present in southern Buenos Aires Province (Yepes 1928) but recent surveys suggest that it is now extinct in this area (Abba and Vizcaíno 2008, 2011; Abba et al. 2012). The reason for its disappearance from Buenos Aires is unknown, but may be related to climate. It ranges from sea level up to 800 m asl (Argentina).
documentation.population:
Few data are available about the abundance of Tolypeutes matacus. It was previously abundant in most xeric parts of the Paraguayan Chaco and Bolivia (Redford and Eisenberg 1992, Meritt 2008, Noss et al. 2010, Aguirre et al. 2019), but field workers in the area have reported a decline in recent years, at least in the Paraguayan subpopulations (P. Smith pers. comm. 2024). More than 20 years ago, it was recorded at densities of 1.9 animals per km² in the Bolivian Chaco (Cuéllar 2002) and of 0.28 animals per km² in the Pantanal of Mato Grosso in Brazil (Schaller 1983). There are no population data of this armadillo in Argentina, but based on the higher number of presence records, higher genetic diversity (Ferreiro et al. 2023) and comments from locals, it is thought to have a higher abundance in the provinces of Chaco and Formosa. The wild population is decreasing, mainly due to intense hunting and habitat loss.

Although no data exist on the longevity of wild individuals, generation length has been estimated at four years based on an extrapolation from other armadillo species.
documentation.habitats: This armadillo, which can roll into a ball when threatened, is found in areas of dry vegetation within the Chaco (Bolkovic et al. 1995). Although capable of digging its own burrows (Attias et al. 2015), it often uses abandoned burrows of other species or hides in dense vegetation. It has a slow reproductive rate; the females give birth to a single young per litter and per year. Its generation length has been estimated at four years; this estimate is based on an extrapolation from other armadillo species.
documentation.threats:
Tolypeutes matacus is threatened by hunting for food. In Santiago del Estero, Argentina, it was found to constitute 55% of the wild fauna in the diet of local people. In the Argentine Chaco it made up 18.4% of the diet of local people and was consumed a mean of 16.5 days per year (+/-1.07) (Altrichter 2006). In Bolivia it is the second most hunted armadillo species by the Izoceño indigenous group, contributing 2% of their total diet.

As it is less fossorial than other species and often active by day, it is easier to hunt than other armadillo species. It is also threatened by habitat destruction through conversion of suitable habitat to cultivated land; however, it is able to adapt to low levels of agricultural disturbance. This species is exported to zoos and, especially, for the pet trade, and there is a high mortality of individuals during this export process. It is sometimes killed on roads. The slow reproductive rate suggests that it may struggle to recover from steep population declines.
documentation.measures: Tolypeutes matacus has been recorded from a number of protected areas but with no more than 12% of its suitable area under protection (Ferreiro 2022; A. Ferreiro pers. comm. 2024). There is a Population Management Plan in place for the captive populations in North American and European zoos.
documentation.use_trade: This armadillo is heavily hunted for food and used as a pet species, especially by indigenous groups both within its range and in other countries. It is also used to make handicrafts. In Bolivia, overhunting and habitat destruction present a worrying threat to the species (Noss et al. 2010). In 2010, Paraguay established quotas for harvesting this species for export abroad under the Proyecto de Conservación y Utilización de la Vida Silvestre, and landowners received a payment for each individual captured on their land (P. Smith pers. comm. 2024). However, captive breeding programmes in the USA have reduced the need to import wild-caught three-banded armadillos especially to zoos, which has reduced hunting pressure.
documentation.rationale: Tolypeutes matacus is listed as Near Threatened because this species is probably in significant decline (albeit at a rate of less than 30% over 12 years) because of widespread habitat loss through much of its range, and because of exploitation for food, thus making the species close to qualifying for Vulnerable under criterion A2cd.
